Mars Hill Church in Seattle, with about 15 locations, dissolved after its founding pastor resigned, and its structure gave no body above the founder the power to act sooner.

slides.head: 7 · Persecution to Solidarity to Insulation to Unaccountability
slides.intro: Genuine cultural hostility toward evangelicals is cited to convert a question about the budget into an attack on Jesus.
items: Persecution narratives and culture-war panic are preached as spiritual danger.
A question is recast as division. Ask about the budget and you have a spirit of division; ask about the allegation and you are touching the anointed.
The person asking is labeled divisive, bitter or in rebellion, often from the platform.
Members close ranks. Loyal members defend the pastor, and several people ask the questioner for coffee with the same message: forgive, stop gossiping, trust leadership.
The question goes unanswered, and "We are financially accountable" stands beside a Senate inquiry that most of the ministries it examined declined to answer in full.

slides.head: 7 · Persecution to Solidarity to Insulation to Unaccountability
rows: 27 · Manufactured Crisis, 17 · Smear Campaign, 16 · Flying Monkeys, 11 · Projection, 12 · DARVO.
Each new question can be read as more proof of hostility, so the questions strengthen the solidarity that shields the institution from them.

It weakens when the question comes from inside. The full record notes that much of the reporting that exposed the pattern came from the evangelical press itself, and the full record closes on the tradition's own principle, the priesthood of all believers, as a warrant to examine the books. This paragraph is analysis, not a documented finding.
The Guidepost report found that the Southern Baptist Executive Committee had treated survivors as adversaries and liabilities while it kept a private list of accused ministers.

slides.head: What they say, what the record shows
rows: Most of the ministries examined by a Senate inquiry declined to provide full disclosure, and the inquiry ended without penalties.
We would never silence a victim.
Departing staff at several large churches, among them Mars Hill, Harvest Bible Chapel, Hillsong and Willow Creek, signed non-disclosure agreements covering leadership conduct.
We have no hierarchy — every believer is a priest.
Founder-pastors hold more unchecked authority than any bishop in this codex, precisely because there is no hierarchy above them.

slides.head: What they say, what the record shows (cont.)
rows: There is no registry because of legal risk.
A list of accused ministers was maintained privately while the registry was opposed publicly.

slides.head: Accountability or theatre?
rows: There were four major collapses in a decade. Three founders resigned and one had died before the findings. This page records no change in network-level governance.
Founder-pastors and network apostles hold it, with appointed boards and no external audit.
The next fall will be revealed by a podcast, the church will dissolve into a new corporate name, and the model will be taught at a leadership conference within a year.

slides.head: Words used here
rows: Inside: It is a scriptural phrase used to shield leaders from criticism. What it does: It is the single most cited verse in this volume, deployed almost exclusively when a leader is under scrutiny and almost never at any other time. Said plainly: 'Do not examine the pastor.'

Inside: It is the formal process for addressing a member's sin. What it does: It frequently arrives at the member raising a concern rather than at the conduct the concern was about, which reverses the direction of accountability entirely. Said plainly: 'You raised something and now you are the subject.'

slides.head: Words used here (cont.)
rows: Inside: It is a program that returns a fallen leader to ministry. What it does: It is almost always applied to leaders and almost never to members, and it is typically administered by the leader's own peers on a timeline nobody outside chose. Said plainly: 'He will be back, and the people he harmed do not have a vote on when.'

Inside: It means causing disunity in the body. What it does: It is a serious charge in congregational polity, applicable to anyone who raises anything in public, and effectively unanswerable. Said plainly: 'You said it where others could hear.'

slides.head: The ledger of exit
rows: The church supplied friends, childcare, school, a small group, and often employment. The denial: "They're free to go anywhere."
Departing staff and members are labeled divisive, bitter, or 'in sin' from the platform. The denial: "We shared only what the congregation needed to know."
Staff leave with severance conditioned on silence. The denial: "Standard HR practice."
Leavers are warned about backsliding, apostasy, losing covering, or eternal consequence. The denial: "It's love, not manipulation."

slides.head: How the cost is denied
rows: Membership covenants and doctrinal statements are written; money and discipline practice often is not.
Access to platform, leadership, and belonging is the currency, and none of it is documented.
Independent polity means no bishop, no denomination, and no one to appeal to.
'Covering,' 'submission,' 'vision,' and 'unity' are defined by whoever is in charge.

slides.head: How the cost is denied (cont.)
rows: Harm is attributed to one bad pastor or to regional culture, never to structure.
Small-group leaders and lay elders enforce; senior leadership stays clean.
Elder-board confidentiality and NDAs both function as sacred secrecy with legal teeth.
'The door is unlocked' is said by institutions that built every relationship the person has.

posts.title: Part 6: Ledger, who is hurt, cases

slides.title: Who benefits, who pays, and the record
slides.sub: The ledger of benefit and cost, who is hurt most, the people in the middle tiers, and six documented cases.

slides.head: Who benefits
items: Founder-pastors and their families benefit through compensation set by hand-picked boards, housing allowances (the part of a US minister's pay that is exempt from income tax), book deals sold to captive congregations, and speaking circuits. Documented collapses (Mars Hill, Hillsong, Willow Creek, RZIM) repeatedly reveal the same architecture.
Christian broadcasting and publishing conglomerates benefit, and their revenue depends on keeping audiences afraid, mobilized, and giving.
Political operatives benefit by renting evangelical trust through voter-guide operations, donor-list harvesting, and policy shops that convert pulpit access into power.

slides.head: Money out, leverage back
items: American evangelical money funds legislative and legal campaigns abroad against LGBTQ rights and reproductive access, routed through local partners and framed as pro-family aid. Recipients get resources; recipient countries get laws their citizens never debated.

Worship music is a global licensing economy: every congregation that sings a megachurch's catalog pays royalties through the CCLI system. Your church's Sunday morning is another church's revenue line.

Congregational trust is harvested for political operations — voter guides, donor lists, and turnout infrastructure built on pulpit access. Your attendance becomes an asset in a market you never entered.

slides.head: Money out, leverage back (cont.)
items: Short-term mission trips move billions in aggregate and are widely criticized in development literature for serving the participants' formation more than the recipients' needs — help structured around the giver.

slides.head: Who pays
items: Poor and working-class members pay, targeted by prosperity teaching.
Women in complementarian churches pay, and so do abuse survivors routed into reconciliation.
LGBTQ members and youth pay, including those subjected to conversion practices (attempts to change sexual orientation or gender identity).
Church staff pay, because their employment, housing, and reference letters depended on silence.
Volunteers pay, because their unpaid labor funded assets titled to the institution.
Children raised in purity culture and hell teaching pay, and they are now the core of the deconstruction generation.

slides.head: Where the weight lands
rows: Prosperity and seed-faith teaching is aimed hardest at those with least. Compounded by: Many give on fixed incomes, via broadcast, with no local relationship to appeal to.
They are excluded from teaching and eldership, and abuse is routed to reconciliation. Compounded by: It is worse where the counseling pastor is a friend of the accused.
They face exclusion and, in past decades, conversion practices. Compounded by: They face it as minors in households that agree with the exclusion.

slides.head: Where the weight lands (cont.)
rows: Their employment, housing, and references are contingent on silence. Compounded by: They have no transferable credentials outside ministry.
They absorbed purity culture and hell teaching as children and process them as adults. Compounded by: Saying so out loud can bring family estrangement.

slides.head: From The LGBTQ+ Codex
items: Where traditions reversed — Multiple mainline Protestant denominations, liberal Jewish movements, and Unitarian and Quaker bodies have ordained and married LGBTQ members following votes of their own governing bodies.

slides.head: From The Children's Codex
items: Reporting, and the internal-first rule — The Guidepost report on the Southern Baptist Convention (2022) found that executive staff maintained a private list of accused ministers for years while the convention publicly asserted its polity made such a list impossible. The impossibility was a claim; the filing cabinet falsified it.

slides.head: People who carry out the work
paras: Most of the institution's work is done below the founder and the board, by people who see decisions without making them. Small-group leaders, worship leaders, staff, elders and deacons, and Christian school teachers each carry part of the load, and each stands at one point where the next decision could be declined. The table sets out what each tier does, what it sees, what it is asked to do and where it could refuse.

slides.head: What each tier sees and could refuse
rows: Does: Hold the actual pastoral relationships and the flow of information upward. Sees: Every doubt, every marital crisis, every departure before leadership does. Is asked to: Report concerns. Could refuse: Convert a confidence into a report
Does: Produce the emotional architecture of the service. Sees: How deliberately the arc is engineered. Is asked to: Build to the giving moment. Could refuse: Place the appeal at the emotional peak

slides.head: What each tier sees and could refuse (cont.)
rows: Does: Run the operation on modest salaries. Sees: The compensation gap, the discretionary account, the NDA in their own severance. Is asked to: Sign the NDA. Could refuse: Sign a non-disclosure agreement covering conduct rather than commercial information

Does: Formally hold authority they were appointed to by the person they oversee. Sees: That unanimity is expected before the meeting starts. Is asked to: Present a united front. Could refuse: Approve a budget line they cannot explain, and say so publicly

slides.head: What each tier sees and could refuse (cont.)
rows: Does: Educate the next cohort. Sees: Which conduct clauses are enforced and against whom. Is asked to: Model the standard. Could refuse: Teach a curriculum they know to be factually false

slides.head: Guidepost report on the Southern Baptist Convention
rows: An independent investigation commissioned under pressure from member churches found that the denomination's Executive Committee had maintained a private list of accused ministers while publicly resisting a registry, and had treated survivors as adversaries and liabilities.

The Executive Committee released its list of accused ministers. Messengers voted in 2022 for a public database; none was ever published, and in 2025 the Executive Committee shelved it, citing legal risk. The list had existed for years without being acted upon.

slides.head: Senate inquiry into six television ministries
rows: A U.S. Senate Finance Committee inquiry examined six large broadcast ministries, documenting private aircraft, high-value parsonages, and boards controlled by the founders' families. Most declined to provide full financial disclosure.
The inquiry concluded without penalties or legislation. The inquiry's principal finding was the sector's opacity — and that opacity remains lawful.

slides.head: A megachurch with no one above the founder (United States, 2014)
rows: Mars Hill Church in Seattle, with about 15 locations, dissolved after its founding pastor resigned amid findings about his leadership.
The church closed; its structure gave no body above the founder the power to act sooner.

slides.head: The apologist's ministry investigates its founder (United States, 2021)
rows: An investigation commissioned by Ravi Zacharias International Ministries found that its late founder had sexually abused massage therapists over years.
The finding came only after the founder's death.

slides.head: The founder, the father and the court (Australia, 2021–2023)
rows: Hillsong founder Brian Houston was charged with concealing his father's child sex offences. He resigned from Hillsong in March 2022 and was found not guilty in August 2023.
Houston was acquitted. He had already stepped down; the verdict did not restore him.

slides.head: Willow Creek: the elder board and the founder (United States, 2018–2019)
rows: Bill Hybels, founding pastor of Willow Creek Community Church near Chicago, resigned in April 2018 after former staff accused him of a pattern of sexually inappropriate words and actions. Willow Creek and Hybels first rebutted the claims. An Independent Advisory Group the church appointed reported in February 2019 that the allegations were credible and faulted the elder board.
The founder had already left; the finding that his accusers were credible came ten months later, from a panel the church chose.

posts.title: Part 7: What can change, and what you can do

slides.title: What can change, and what you can do
slides.sub: Precedent for change, voices from inside, three countries, the questions to ask, how to leave safely, and where to get help.

slides.head: It has been broken before
rows: The SBC's Guidepost report was published in full, and the Executive Committee's list of accused ministers was released.
Who: Survivors and member churches forced the motion. When: 2022. Cost: Advocates faced years of denominational resistance and personal attacks.
Purity culture was repudiated by its own principal authors.
Who: The authors did it themselves, publicly. When: 2016–2019. Cost: Not recorded on this page.
Major ex-gay ministries closed with a public apology.
Who: Former leaders of those ministries closed them. When: 2013. Cost: Exodus International closed.

slides.head: Promises on the record
rows: Southern Baptist Convention — a database of credibly accused ministers

2022, following the Guidepost report. Status: Abandoned. Messengers voted for the "Ministry Check" database in 2022. No name was ever published; in February 2025 the Executive Committee said it was no longer a focus, citing legal hurdles. In August 2026 survivors launched their own national database, ProtestantAccountability.org, with more than 2,700 people accused of committing or covering up church abuse listed at launch.

slides.quote: Public, retroactive release of departing staff from their non-disclosure agreements at the movement's flagship churches would revise the concealment findings — and would cost nothing but the concealment.

slides.head: People who spoke
items: Christa Brown. A survivor and retired lawyer, she wrote to 18 Baptist leaders in four states in 2004–05 to warn them about the youth minister who had abused her, and none of them offered help.

The survivors who built their own database. In 2026, after the Southern Baptist database was shelved, survivors led by Chellee Taylor launched ProtestantAccountability.org in August 2026, a searchable national database of more than 2,700 people accused of committing or covering up church abuse.
Alan Chambers. As president of Exodus International, an ex-gay ministry, he apologized to gay people and shut the ministry down in 2013.
Joshua Harris. The author of I Kissed Dating Goodbye, the best-known book of purity culture, he discontinued his own bestseller in 2018.

slides.head: United States
rows: There is no single apex. Polity is congregational and independent, and the SBC president is elected annually while the executive staff are not.

Churches file no Form 990 (the annual public return other US charities must file). State attorneys general have jurisdiction over charitable assets. Many states exempt clergy from mandatory reporting.
The Guidepost report (2022) examined the SBC. The Grassley Senate inquiry (2007–2011) closed without full disclosure. Megachurch NDA controversies have recurred.

slides.head: United States (cont.)
rows: Exit costs are low socially in most of the country, and high where the church is also the school, employer, and social world, which is common in the South and Midwest.
Complaints go to state attorneys general, and to the IRS for affiliated entities that do file. The SBC messenger vote is a genuine internal lever.
The country with the largest evangelical population has among the weakest religious financial disclosure in the developed world. Those two facts are related.

slides.head: United Kingdom
rows: Authority sits in denominational structures and independent churches. Most are charities, though smaller churches in several denominations are excepted from registration until 2031.
The Charity Commission requires annual accounts, publishes trustee names, and can open statutory inquiries and remove trustees. Serious incident reporting is mandatory.
The Commission has opened statutory inquiries into churches over safeguarding and financial management, and has removed trustees.
Exit costs are generally low, and higher in tightly-knit immigrant and diaspora congregations.

slides.head: United Kingdom (cont.)
rows: The Charity Commission is the most reader-usable regulator in this entire volume. It is free and searchable, and it acts.
The theology and the practices are the same, and the accounts are published. The variable is a disclosure statute.

slides.head: Australia
rows: Authority sits with denominational bodies and independent megachurches, notably in the Hillsong network.

Churches register with the ACNC (the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission), though churches that qualify as "basic religious charities" are exempt from financial reporting. The Royal Commission (2013–2017) covered institutions across denominations. Mandatory reporting varies by state.
The record includes Royal Commission case studies, the Hillsong disclosures, and Brian Houston's 2022 resignation, followed by a 2023 acquittal on the criminal charge.

slides.head: Australia (cont.)
rows: Exit costs are low socially, and higher for those employed in church-linked enterprises.
The ACNC oversees finances and governance. State child-protection authorities and state police are the other routes.
Australia produced the most thorough statutory examination of institutional child abuse anywhere. Its findings are usable by readers in every other jurisdiction.

slides.head: Six questions to ask
items: If there is nothing to hide, why won't your church publish its budget, your pastor's salary, and its housing allowance — on the website, this week?
Why does a church that preaches truth-telling require departing staff to sign non-disclosure agreements?
The last time a leader was accused, who conducted the investigation, who paid them, and did the report get published in full or summarized by the people it examined?
If the door is unlocked, why does everyone who walks through it lose every friend they had?
Prosperity teaching says giving produces return. Ask for the data. Then ask why the only reliably enriched party is the person teaching it.

slides.head: Six questions to ask (cont.)
items: You were told doubt is dangerous and criticism is divisive. Ask who is protected by those two rules, and notice it is never you.

slides.head: The priesthood of all believers
paras: Your tradition's founding claim is the priesthood of all believers — that you can read, interpret, and stand before God without a middleman. Take that seriously and the conclusion is unavoidable: you do not need permission to examine your church's books, its process, or its pastor. That is not rebellion against Protestant principle. It is Protestant principle.

slides.head: The priesthood of all believers (cont.)
paras: The people who exposed Mars Hill, Hillsong, and the SBC's own abuse records were not atheists. They were believers who refused to let loyalty to an institution stand in for loyalty to God. You are allowed to be one of them. You may find it is the most evangelical thing you ever do.

slides.head: Practical guidance, not legal advice
items: Leaving is legally free. The costs are social, family and sometimes economic, where the church is also the school, employer or social world.
If you signed a non-disclosure agreement as staff, it generally cannot stop you reporting a crime to police; take the agreement to a lawyer.
Membership covenants. Some churches ask members to sign one; you can resign membership in writing.
If you were abused, go to the police or child-protection services first, not the church.
Find support that is not run by a church.
